questions.question: Why does the lecturer argue that dynamic programming is not technically an algorithm?
questions.gold_answer: The lecturer explains that dynamic programming is more accurately described as a problem-solving technique rather than a specific algorithm.
questions.quote: Technically speaking, DP is not an algorithm. It's actually a problem solving technique.

questions.question: What is the primary reason the lecturer recommends using assumptions instead of breaking problems into sub-problems?
questions.gold_answer: Breaking problems into sub-problems can become overly mathematical and difficult to understand, whereas making assumptions leverages our natural human tendency to make judgments.
questions.quote: Most people learn to solve DP problems by breaking them into sub-problems. And when you try to do that, the approach becomes quite mathematical and hard to understand. That's why, instead of thinking in terms of sub-problems, I recommend making an assumption.

questions.question: What is the fundamental requirement for the original problem and the assumed problem in dynamic programming?
questions.gold_answer: The original problem and the assumed problem must be somewhat different from each other for the dynamic programming approach to be effective.
questions.quote: The main point I am trying to make here is that the original problem and the assumed problem have to be somewhat different for dynamic programming to work.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the recursive rule in the context of the longest-increasing subsequence problem?
questions.gold_answer: The recursive rule formalizes the logic of checking all previous indices to see if a current number can extend an existing subsequence to create a longer one.
questions.quote: Recursive rule is just a fancy way of formalizing what we have already discussed. To find the length of the longest-increasing subsequence ending at the current last index, we go through all the indices to the left of it.

questions.question: How does the lecturer define the base case for the longest-increasing subsequence problem?
questions.gold_answer: The base case is defined by initializing the length of the longest-increasing subsequence ending at any index to 1, because each individual number is a subsequence of length 1.
questions.quote: Each number by itself can be seen as a subsequence of length 1, ending at its own index. And this subsequence is an increasing subsequence because it has only one number. So the initial length for the longest-increasing subsequence ending at any index would be 1.

questions.question: What is the final step in determining the answer to the longest-increasing subsequence problem once the array of lengths is populated?
questions.gold_answer: To get the final answer, you take the maximum value found in the array that stores the lengths of the longest-increasing subsequences ending at every index.
questions.quote: Now for the answer of the original question, we don't care about which index the subsequence ends at. So we take the maximum of longest subsequence ending at every index and that would be our final answer.

questions.question: How does the implementation handle the process of considering an increasing number of elements from the input array?
questions.gold_answer: An outer for loop is used to incrementally consider more numbers from the array, starting from the first two and ending at the last index.
questions.quote: Now we have a for loop that decides how many numbers of the array are we considering at the current time. In the beginning, we are considering only the first two numbers. So we start the loop at the index 1. In the end, we want to consider all the numbers.

questions.question: Why is it important to know the ending number of a subsequence when solving the longest-increasing subsequence problem?
questions.gold_answer: Knowing the ending number is necessary to determine if a new number can be added to the end of the existing subsequence to extend it.
questions.quote: If you remember, we compared 3 to the highest number in the longest subsequence so far to decide whether the subsequence can be expanded by adding 3 to it. So knowing where a subsequence ends is very important to solve this problem
